claim_text: Hex says an unauthorized third party ran commands on its web servers on Nov 23
summary: Hex says: 'On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers.' It says it blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes.
detail: Hex published its post on Nov 24 and says it will update it as its investigation continues.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Hex's own incident post states it.

claim_text: The flaw let anyone send a crafted request, without signing in, that ended in running commands; it had been in the code since 2016
summary: Hex says hex.pm decoded request bodies in an Erlang data format before checking who sent them, and a chain of crafted values ended in running operating system commands. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-129514.
detail: Hex says 69 malicious requests arrived between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC, and commands ran on six web servers, three of them because a restart brought up servers still on the old build. It says the safety check in the decoder was removed on Feb 23, 2016. Every server was on a fixed build by 18:31 UTC.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Hex's post describes the flaw, the timeline and the servers affected.

claim_text: Who did it is not known
summary: Hex does not name the attacker, and we found no claim of responsibility. The Hacker News (the outlet) also says who was behind it is unknown.
detail: We did not open leak or dark-web sites.
label: Not established

claim_text: Hex says the attacker seems to have built a copy of hex.pm to test against beforehand
summary: Hex says it found repeated downloads of hex.pm's own dependencies from the attacker's two addresses since Nov 19, which 'suggests the attacker built a local copy of hex.pm to test against'.
detail: Hex also says a separate security report describing the same flaw reached it by email at 19:07 UTC on Nov 23, after the attack had ended. It does not say who sent it or link it to the attacker.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Hex's own reading of its logs; nobody outside has checked it.

claim_text: Hex says it found no sign that packages were changed, that its database was changed, or that the attacker kept access
summary: Hex says: 'We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems.' Nobody outside Hex has checked.
detail: Hex says all 23 releases published during the incident match its audit log, no older release changed, and every package file written since 18:00 UTC matches the checksums in its database. It compared every row of its database with a copy from before the attack. It says documentation archives have no checksum to compare against.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Hex's own checks; The Hacker News repeats them from Hex's post, so it is not a separate check.

claim_text: Hex cannot rule out that account data in its database was read
summary: Hex says database reads are not logged, so it cannot rule out that the attacker read email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, two-factor (2FA) secrets, sessions and audit logs.
detail: Hex says passwords are hashed with bcrypt, which slows guessing but does not prevent it for a weak password, so it asks users to change theirs.
label: Confirmed

claim_text: Reads of private packages and documentation cannot be fully ruled out; Hex will contact affected organisations
summary: Hex says reads of private packages during the attack match releases their owners made at the time, but a read from a compromised server would look the same. 'We will contact affected organizations directly.'
detail: Hex says its delivery network logs show no requests from the attacker's addresses to private documentation in the last 30 days, but direct reads from its cloud storage are not logged.
label: Confirmed

claim_text: Hex is not asking users to replace API keys, saying the stored hashes cannot be reversed
summary: Hex says API keys are 128-bit random values stored only as hashes, which it considers far beyond brute force, so it does not see a need to rotate them.
detail: This is Hex's own judgement; we found no outside assessment of it.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Hex's own reasoning, not checked by anyone else.

claim_text: Hex replaced its server credentials and signing keys and signed everyone out
summary: Hex says it replaced the storage, delivery network, email and database credentials its servers used, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. 'This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients.'
detail: By 10:42 UTC on Nov 24 it had replaced every credential the attacker could have read except the registry signing key and a few low-impact secrets. It says it is building a new registry signing system that supports replacing that key, with new Hex client releases in the coming days.
label: Confirmed

claim_text: Hex reported the breach to the Swedish data protection authority, CISA and ENISA on Nov 23
summary: Hex says it reported a personal data breach to IMY, the Swedish data protection authority, reported the incident to CISA in the US, and sent an early warning to ENISA, the EU cybersecurity agency, on the evening of Nov 23 (UTC).
detail: Hex gives 22:58, 23:05 and 23:26 UTC. It says CISA confirmed receipt. We found no public statement from any of the three.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Hex's own post gives the times.

claim_text: Hex asks account holders to change their password, reset 2FA and update the Hex client, and to fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm
summary: Hex asks users to change their hex.pm password, set up two-factor authentication again with a new secret, and update their Hex client when the release with the new signing system is out. Until then: do not trust third-party mirrors.
detail: Hex also warns that email addresses may have been exposed, so emails claiming to come from Hex should be checked: links should lead to hex.pm.
label: Confirmed

claim_text: People who only download public packages and never made an account have nothing to reset
summary: The Hacker News reports that one of the post's authors said, on the Elixir Forum, that developers who never created a hex.pm account and only fetch public packages have nothing to reset.
detail: Those who signed up with GitHub should still sign in to their clients again, and reset 2FA if they enabled it. The forum thread is where the question was asked and answered; it is not cited as evidence on its own.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: The Hacker News reports the clarification and the forum thread shows it was made there.

claim_text: Which organisations use Hex, and whether any were affected, is not publicly known
summary: Hex names no customers, and no organisation has said publicly that it was affected. Hex says it will contact affected organisations directly. Its home page says it counted 11,586,768 package downloads the day before we looked.
detail: Where we looked on Nov 26: Hex's own site (its sponsors page lists companies that provide services to Hex, which are suppliers, not users; its pricing page names no customers), SEC filings from Nov 20 to Nov 26 (none names hex.pm), and news reporting (no outlet names an affected organisation). The Elixir language's own site lists companies that use Elixir, which fetches packages from Hex by default, but those pages do not say the companies use Hex, so we do not name them here. We do not search code or guess from other sites.
label: Not established
why_it_supports: Hex's own site names no customers, and its post names no affected organisation.
